title: Blogging Platform
seoTitle: Design a Blogging Platform Like Medium
description: Design a blogging platform — writing and publishing posts with drafts, serving read-heavy articles fast via caching and static rendering, comments, and follower feeds.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Blogging Platform?
blocks.text: A blogging platform like Medium or WordPress.com lets writers draft and publish articles, and lets readers read, comment on and follow writers.

items: Writers should be able to create drafts, edit them, and publish posts with images.
Readers should be able to read published posts by URL.
Readers should be able to comment on posts.
Readers should be able to follow writers and see a feed of new posts.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Extremely read-heavy (1000:1); post pages load in < 200ms worldwide.
Highly available reads; publishing can take a few seconds to propagate.
Drafts must never be lost while writing.
**Post**: author, title, slug, body (rich text / markdown), status (draft/published), timestamps.

blocks.text: The editor autosaves to the **Post Service** every few seconds, storing revisions so nothing is lost. Images upload directly to blob storage via presigned URLs. Publishing marks the post published and triggers rendering.

Published posts rarely change, so render them to HTML at publish time (or on first request) and serve them from a **CDN**. Edits re-render and purge that URL. Dynamic bits (comment counts, "you follow this author") load separately via small API calls.
Comments are stored per post and loaded via the API with cursor pagination, cached briefly per post since most readers see the same first page.
When a writer publishes, a worker adds the post to followers' feeds (fan-out on write is fine — publishing is rare compared to reading), stored as capped lists in a cache.
1) How do we serve posts fast to a global audience?

blocks.title: Render from the database on every request

approach.text: Query the post and render HTML per page view.

challenges.text: Wasted work at 1000:1 read ratios and slow for distant readers.

approach.text: Cache rendered HTML in Redis near the app servers.

challenges.text: Faster, but readers far from the region still pay network latency.

blocks.title: Static rendering + CDN with targeted purge

approach.text: Generate HTML at publish time (incremental static regeneration), cache it at the CDN edge with long TTLs, and purge just that URL on edits. Personalised fragments load client-side so the page itself stays cacheable for everyone.

challenges.text: Purge latency means an edit may take seconds to appear everywhere — acceptable here.

blocks.text: 2) How do we never lose a draft?

Autosave frequently with small diffs, store revisions server-side with optimistic concurrency (a version number) to detect conflicting edits from two tabs, and keep a local copy in the browser so writing continues offline and syncs when the connection returns.

quiz.question: Why render posts to HTML at publish time?
options: Posts are read far more than written, so render once and serve many times
quiz.explanation: Pre-rendered pages are cheap to cache and serve.

quiz.question: How do you keep post pages cacheable while showing personalised info?
options: Load personalised fragments separately via small API calls
Use cookies in the cache key
quiz.explanation: The page stays identical for everyone; personalised bits load client-side.

quiz.question: Why is fan-out on write fine for follower feeds here?
options: Publishing is rare compared to reading
quiz.explanation: Infrequent publishes keep write amplification affordable.

quiz.question: What protects drafts from being lost?
options: Frequent autosave with server-side revisions and a local copy
quiz.explanation: Revisions plus local persistence survive crashes and disconnects.
